draft.title: Bush foods and products from Country
card: Some First Nations businesses make food, skin care and medicines from native plants. Examples are products made with finger lime, Kakadu plum or wattleseed.
These businesses draw on knowledge about plants that First Nations peoples have held for thousands of years. This knowledge was passed on over many generations.
Cultural knowledge belongs to the people who hold it. A business may protect how it is used by setting rules about who can share it and who can make products from it.
Many of these businesses work with the community that holds the knowledge. They may also share the money earned with that community.
draft.remember: Bush food businesses turn knowledge of native plants into products, and they protect how that knowledge is used.

a.q: Which of these is a First Nations bush food and product business?
opts: A firm making skin care from Kakadu plum, guided by Elders
A shop selling imported olive oil from Europe
A factory making soft drinks with artificial flavours
A farm growing wheat for export using modern seed
a.why: Only the first option uses native plants and knowledge held by First Nations peoples. The wheat farm is a farm, but it does not use that knowledge or make products from native plants.
a.clue: Look for native plants and knowledge from Country.

b.q: Daniel's community business makes tea from a native plant, using knowledge from Elders. Why might it set rules about who can use that knowledge?
opts: The knowledge belongs to the community, so it guards its use
Rules make the tea cheaper for the business to produce
Native plants cannot be sold unless rules are in place
Knowledge held for many years has no use in business
b.why: The knowledge belongs to the people who hold it, so they can decide how it is used. Rules do not make the tea cheaper, and the card does not say that native plants cannot be sold without rules.
b.clue: Think about who the knowledge belongs to.

a.best: A firm making skin care from Kakadu plum, guided by Elders

b.best: The knowledge belongs to the community, so it guards its use

a.q: Which business draws on First Nations knowledge of native plants?
opts: Makes balm from native plants, using what Elders teach
Makes jam from finger lime, using a recipe its chef invented
Makes soap from olive oil, using an old Greek family recipe
Makes bread from wheat, using a method passed down for ages
a.why: The balm business uses native plants and knowledge passed on by Elders. The finger lime jam uses a native plant, but its recipe was invented by a chef, so it does not draw on First Nations knowledge.
a.clue: You need both a native plant and knowledge held by First Nations peoples.

Knowledge held for many years has no use in business
b.why: The knowledge belongs to the people who hold it, so they can decide how it is used. Rules are about protecting that knowledge, not about making the tea cheaper, and native plants can be sold without such rules.
b.clue: Think about who the knowledge belongs to.
